text: A million years ago, battery chargers used something called a "synchronous rectifier." A solenoid, driven by the magnetic field within the step-down transformer, moved a set of switch contacts back and forth in phase with the AC (hence "synchronous") and these contacts literally switched polarity of the AC connections between the transformer and the battery being charged. text:
Active rectification looking "good" has more to do with voltage than current. For example, the 12V to ~1V DC-DC converter in every modern computer's motherboard that powers the CPU would at best be about 70% efficient if it had to use a diode as the output rectifier simply because even the best modern low-voltage, high-current Schottky diodes will drop around 0.4V and that's a substantial portion of the output voltage. These days, those converters exclusively use active rectification. It also helps that low voltage MOSFETs are much better suited for active rectification than high-voltage MOSFETs and the circuitry for driving a low-side active rectifier (which that circuit uses) is much cheaper than a high-side rectifier. This is why the 2206 in the video even exists, it has a much simpler driving circuit than the 2208.

AC mains, even in the USA, is at least about 120V and diodes used for it tend to drop between 0.6V and 1.1V. Even with two diodes, that's a much smaller percentage of the voltage than in the above example. ATX power supplies almost never use active rectification on any of the high voltage sides. The few that have active rectifiers in the AC input are far more expensive than similarly rated standard efficiency power supplies and that's for a relatively small efficiency improvement. Even then, those power supplies use a totem-pole converter with silicon carbide or gallium nitride MOSFETs, not a silicon MOSFET H-bridge followed by a boost PFC circuit. A large part of their still relatively small efficiency gain is the fact that they eliminated the boost circuit's output rectifier completely instead of just going to active rectification.

​ @andreystya6644  If you meant that a MOSFET rated for 25A will require higher gate drive current than a smaller MOSFET rated at 10A, that's true if you want to switch them at the same frequency. That said, MOSFETs are typically used far below their max current rating and gate drive current isn't a big problem here unless you want extremely fast switching frequencies. AC-DC PFC circuits tend to use low enough switching frequencies that gate drive current isn't a big problem (usually less than 100KHz). Assuming you have a MOSFET rated at 25A or more, you don't need more gate drive current to conduct 25A than to conduct 10A with the same MOSFET if you have the MOSFET fully on. If you charge GS enough for DS to be fully on, DS will happily pass any current you want, even if you pass so much current that it heats up until it smokes and/or blows up.

GS is a capacitor. GS doesn't pass much DC current once it is charged up to the driver circuit's max voltage. Increasing the driving current going to GS allows you to switch it on and off faster by charging and discharging its capacitance faster, but that doesn't change how much current DS can conduct while on. Another consequence of GS being a capacitor is that the current used to charge it can be recovered and returned to the power source instead of being discharged to ground if using a resonant gate driver circuit. That's more expensive than a typical gate driver, further demonstrating that chasing every small improvement in power converter efficiency comes with exponentially increasing costs.

Also, silicon carbide and especially gallium nitride transistors have low gate capacitance and have much lower gate drive current requirements than similarly rated silicon transistors.

text: Well, the good news is that in full wave 3 phase rectification using 6 diodes only 2 diodes (or no diodes) are conducting at any given time so, using your numbers the power being dissipated would be (0.6V X 2) X 100 Amps or 120 watts.  It doesn't really work that way though...  The bad news is that at high currents silicon rectifiers drop much more than 0.6 volts.  It is not uncommon to see 1.0 volt to 1.5 volts (look at the Vf curves on a 1N400X data sheet...) forward voltage drop across a silicon diode when conducting high currents - which is the case in most rectification systems because the conduction angle of the diodes is much less than 180 degrees (single phase) or 60 degrees in a 3 phase system.  Since the diodes are not conducting continuously, and the output current is a continuous 100 amps (in your example) it follows that when the diodes ARE conducting the peak current must be MUCH higher than 100 amps in order to provide an average 100 amp output current.  These high current pulses (near the maximum voltage of the AC input) result in a much higher RMS current in the rectifiers than you would expect which causes a lot more heating than you would expect - requiring a much larger diode than you would expect if you are to have a reliable circuit.

text: This is how HVDC converters work on the power grid! You take 3-phase AC, run it through a wye and a delta transformer to get 12 poles (6 pairs of phase). You then feed them to an active element, triggering at the right point. In the old days, it was mercury valves, then it moved to thyristors, and these days they're often IGBT (Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistors). For HVDC applications, these are huge, dwarfing a human. Voltage differences of up to a million volts kinda needs some room. Modern designs use stacks of them for each pole, switched at different times to match sine waves, minimizing ripple in magnitude and raising it in frequency, so it can be filtered with smaller capacitors + inductors. The 3.4 GW Pacific Intertie uses thyristors now, originally mercury valves when it was placed into service in 1970 (originally at 1.4 GW). The newer Transbay link under San Francisci bay uses IGBTs. HVDC links between England and Europe, Tasmania and South Australia, US/Canada and US/Mexico. In some places, there are back-to-back pairs to isolate different AC grids from each other; Japan has 4 like this, with 60 Hz on one side and 50 Hz on the other. It's the same circuitry on each side, whether used as an inverter or an AC-DC converter. Which direction the power flows comes down to the phase angle of the triggering signals. So solar and wind use them as inverters, while grid batteries use them in both modes.

7:31 The simplest and most likely answer may be to observe that a capacitor initially looks like a dead short.  I can't see the size of the caps you're using, but they look big enough that it will look like a short for long enough to blow that fuse.  This will be at least partly why the datasheet stipulates the use of a boost converter on the rectifier's output.  A naïve boost converter will present a mostly inductive load at its input, so there is no high initial inrush current in quite the same way.  Real boost converters will still have some C on their input in order to control EMC, but not as much as you're trying to load the rectifier with.


Beyond that, another possible answer, and this is just a guess, is that these IRF740 FETs are just too slow and chunky for this application.  As you noted, if a third FET is still partially conducting, you'll get a low impedance path that might look like enough of a short to blow the fuse.  There are two parameters worth looking at that might explain how that situation could arise, even with the TEA2208 controller: gate charge and conduction recovery time.  

As you probably know, 1) a FET's gate is a capacitor and 2) the gate voltage that matters is that relative to the FET's source pin (ie Vgs), which is not always ground.  Especially for the high side FETs, the controller has to be able to drive a sufficient Vgs relative to its own ground to turn it on†, but that voltage will be different from that relative to the controller's own ground.  So, usually, the controller needs a charge pump to get the required Vgs.  The current capacity of this charge pump affects how quickly it can turn the FET on and off, so a FET that stores more charge on its gate will take longer to switch.  Contrast the specs for the IRF740 with a better power FET like On Semi NTMFS5H600NL.

Recovery time is probably not relevant for a sinusoidal input at these frequencies, but it's worth remembering that a FET doesn't stop conducting immediately after Vgs goes away.

† "on" can mean "in linear/triode region" or "in saturation".  These terms are also used with bipolar transistors but, unhelpfully, their meanings are reversed.  For FETs used as switches, you want the smallest possible drop across the FET itself, which means operating the FET in its triode region (Vgs > Vt, Vds < Vgs-Vt, noting again that Vds the voltage across the channel, not relative to ground).

From a purely theoretical standpoint, the fact that there are more components involved with the active circuit means that the MTBF (Mean Time Before Failure) will be shorter with the switching circuit than with the diodes.  However, in real life it comes   down to the specific design of each circuit and how hot each of the components get - typically a 10 degree C rise means roughly half the service life.   Assuming there is enough space and / or airflow to keep everything cool enough, it shouldn't be hard to get the circuit to last for decades of normal use.

For anything attached to AC mains however, a big killer is lightning surges that make it into the house.  So the limiting factor is how much surge protection is available before those circuits, and the voltage ratings of the devices attached to the mains.

text:
I've got a BSEE. The correct name is "Full Wave Bridge" or "Full Wave Rectifier". This is in contrast to a "Half-Wave Rectifier" (a simple diode). It has that name because it allows the full incoming AC wave to be transferred to the load. Also, a full-wave bridge is usually drawn as it is because of its similarity to a Wheatstone Bridge (often used to monitor sensors such as strain gauges and solid-state thermometers).

The voltage drop across a semiconductor diode is 0.7v for common technologies. That's constant regardless of the current flowing through the device (until it burns up). There are two diode-drops in each path through the full-wave bridge. With a 120V p-p AC input, that means that the power loss is about 1.17%. Every component involved in any circuit uses power (generally expressed as heat). So the extra components added for your alternative themselves use power. When you start with an energy savings "budget" of just 1.17%, it isn't surprising that you end up with little savings to show for the effort.

This exercise sounds like what we programmers (I'm now a programmer) call "premature optimization".

I was not surprised that you ultimately found that a full-wave bridge is nearly always a solid engineering choice.

text:
Not mentioned in the video is that all SMPS perform rectification at least twice, and this test only replaced the mains rectification stage where potential efficiency gains are usually negligible. Active rectification gains are most significant on the low side which is why almost all reasonably sophisticated power supplies do it. Pretty much any SMPS with PFC will already have active rectification.

There's way more to active rectifiers than this video covers such as the design and operation of the charge pumps and level shifters for the gate drivers and the relative (and often hidden) efficiency cost of gate drive current on power factor versus the typical diode junction capacitance of a standard rectifier.

This type of active rectification mainly applies to power electronics but there is also a whole other genre of small signal "precision" rectifiers whose designs are equally interesting. And really the mercury-arc rectifier is the king of cool as rectifiers go. An impossible act to follow.

text:
I see this video is a year old and has a ton of comments, so probably someone has already raised this issue.  One huge difference between between the diode bridge and the MOSFET bridge is that the diode bridge only allows current flow in one direction (input -> output), where the MOSFET bridge allows current flow in both directions (input <-> output).  This is why the fuse blew with the large capacitive load, since large currents are flowing in and out of the load capacitor.  This can be addressed by using a fancier gate controller that shuts off one of the MOSFETs when the input voltage drops below the voltage on the output load capacitor.  This can work ok at 50/60Hz mains frequency with clean waveforms, but gets much more difficult at higher frequencies.

The MOSFET bridge is actually an old idea.  I've simpler circuits (no controller IC) that use two N-channel MOSFETs and two P-channel MOSFETs with the gates simply cross-coupled directly to the input.  This circuit was sometimes used to allow a low-voltage DC-input device to work independently of the polarity of the DC input voltage, which was handy since barrel connectors could be either center-positive or center-negative.  It still had the problem of blowing the input fuse if connected to an AC input, though.

Likewise increasing the conductive area on a single diode also will not decrease its  junction voltage drop. If you don't believe me then try a diode test on a DVM with a single diode and then multiple diodes in parallel. I am not a fan off MOSFETs in power circuits, because they tend to fail closed, or sometimes blow apart. If they failed open that would be better. text: Power factor correction is real.  I blew many triacs using zero crossing detectors while trying to drive inductive loads.  Let me break that down.  A triac is like an AC mosfet, it can conduct in both directions, but when the voltage goes to zero, you have to "turn it back on" and this happens 60 times a second with mains voltage.  The zero crossing detector will detect when mains or AC voltage crosses from plus to minus or minus to plus, to turn the triac on.  For resistive loads, this works like a charm.  Any time I attached something with a power factor, my triacs would break, and stay permanently closed/fused.  This included power tools with motors, or large CRTs (Cathode Ray Tubes, computer screens of the previous millennium), or anything with a large power factor aka inductive load.  This is because, while current and voltage are in-phase for resistive loads, they got out of phase in inductive loads, so my zero crossing detector would try to go off while current was flowing through the triac.  Bang, triac dead.  GreatScott, a video on this effect would be very useful.  Also a full bridge rectifier does not suffer from a power factor / inductive load, since it is a passive component, and thus a good choice.  Even linear regulators like the venerable 7805 have a place where rock steady voltage is required, like audio projects.

text:
Nice very basic electronics video. Looking at a year of comments and only seeing one or two that hit the 'sweet spot', which is Heat and Efficiency.
One heat: It is an electronics killer. Every 10°C. increase in temperature doubles the rate of failure for anything electronic . How many hours do you want the circuit to perform correctly? Cool it 10° C and you double the life to 'mean failure' (based on Military and Commercial Standards).
You covered the efficiency nicely. A diode has a fixed voltage drop at the current rate being used. At lower voltages, that drop becomes important! If you use a bridge, each side has two diodes which increase the problem. A single diode half wave (or steering diode) is better efficiency than a full wave bridge, but if power is reversed the circuit does not work. That makes it a 'design choice' and you need to prioritize your needs. 
Be aware, adding more electronic components decrease that system's reliability. Based on the system's mission, that may become a huge factor. Oh, generally the more components the higher the system cost.
These are common issues for a system based design and only one choice is not a good answer., you need a bag full.

text: Good video.  Active rectifiers have been known since the 1980s, and we used these in some satellite applications where low voltage batteries were being used.  The main problem with FETs is that the higher the voltage standoff, the higher the source/drain resistance.  FETs now are up to about 1000+volts and IGBTs are over 4000+volts, but in both cases the loss voltage across the device is almost proportional, so still requires roughly the same cooling power, for the given application.  We did railroad applications at 2000+volts, 500+amps, where we had to use antifreeze liquid for cooling, in specially milled tubes inside of the heatsinks.  Freon and chilled water cooling was also tried, but these has significant physical disadvantages, and had poor heat transfer under unusual or incorrect operating conditions, often resulting in catastrophic failures.  Our ten-ton experimental 6-wheel truck would often burst into flames, with such failures.  In thermal world, "there is no free lunch".  You must cool adequately, for any given power level, period, or burst into flames.  Your example is good for a "few" watts of loss, and then it will cook itself, since the heat outflow is very low.

text:
This was weirdly unsatisfying. You've shown all the wrong application for this circuit and some of the information provided was also a bit confusing. First of all, it's not really the current, it's the voltage drop on those diodes compared to mains voltage. If you have around 0.56V drop on each diode, there are two in series and you are trying to rectify 25V, of course the efficiency lost on these diodes will be 100%*(0.56*2)/25 = 4,5%. The higher the rectified voltage, the less of an effect that drop will have. Try doing the same thing with 12V or 5V... 
An 100A diode will still have around 1V drop below 20A, so you can make something that will be reasonably efficient even with extremely high current. The problem is that these components are very expencive. You can also use shottky diodes and there are some power modules with extreme performance, like the 300CNQ045PbF, which has 0.61V drop at 150A, it just costs around $45.
Active rectifiers solve specific problem, which is when you need to rectify low voltage with somewhat high current.
